sections.title: What is First-Principles Thinking?
sections.content: First-principles thinking means breaking down a complex problem into its most basic, undeniable truths and reasoning up from there. Instead of arguing by analogy ('this is like X'), you build your argument from fundamental facts.
bullets: Identify the fundamental truths that everyone agrees on
Break assumptions down until you reach bedrock facts
Rebuild your argument from those facts upward

sections.title: Why It Wins Debates
sections.content: Most debaters argue by analogy — comparing their case to something familiar. First-principles thinking is harder to counter because it does not rely on assumptions. It reveals hidden flaws in conventional wisdom.
bullets: Analogy: 'Tax cuts worked in the 1980s, so they will work now'
First-principles: 'What are the actual current economic conditions? What specific mechanisms would make tax cuts effective today?'
First-principles arguments are harder to rebut because they are built on unshakeable foundations

options: 'This policy worked in Sweden, so it will work here'
'What are the fundamental economic forces at play, and how will this policy interact with them?'
'My opponent is wrong because experts disagree'
sections.feedback: First-principles breaks down to fundamental truths rather than relying on analogies or authority.

sections.q: What distinguishes first-principles thinking from arguing by analogy?
options: First-principles breaks down to basic truths; analogy compares to similar situations
sections.explain: First-principles reasoning starts from fundamental truths. Analogies compare the current situation to past ones, which may not apply.

sections.sentence: First-principles thinking breaks problems down to their most basic, {0} truths.
sections.feedback: First-principles reasoning starts from truths that cannot be disputed.

sections.statement: Arguing by analogy is just as reliable as first-principles thinking.
sections.feedback: Analogies can be misleading because no two situations are identical. First-principles reasoning is more rigorous.

questions.scenario: In a debate about implementing a four-day work week, the opposition argues 'This failed in the past.'
questions.question: How would a first-principles response differ?
options: Analyze the specific conditions that caused past failure and whether they apply today
Cite a study showing it works now
questions.feedback: First-principles examines the specific mechanisms and conditions rather than relying on past outcomes.
